issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette:
Since the exposure, Kwame, a 62-year-old bomb disposal technician, has described his world as permanently edged with danger. The incident happened at work during what had first seemed like a controlled response to a suspicious device in an industrial setting. When the container was opened, it released a toxic chemical plume before the team could fully contain it. He remembers the sharp, sterile-burning smell in the air, the confusion of shouted instructions, and the abrupt sense that his own body had become unsafe terrain. In the aftermath he was taken through medical evaluation, surrounded by antiseptic odors and emergency activity that have remained fused in his mind with the moment he realized he might not be able to protect himself. What stays vivid for him is not only the exposure itself, but the feeling that danger was invisible, already in the air, and could reach him before he had time to react.

In the weeks afterward, the workplace itself became charged for him. Entering the facility, hearing sudden loud noises, or catching even a faint hospital or antiseptic smell could pull him into the same tense, immediate alarm. He found that these moments did not just upset him; they changed what he did. He began avoiding medical settings whenever possible, putting off examinations and steering away from hospitals and ambulances because the sights and smells felt too close to the exposure. He also started arranging his days so that he was rarely by himself in a room or building, and when he could not avoid those situations he felt markedly less steady. Most of all, he worked excessively. Staying busy on the job made sense to him because it kept him from sitting alone with the memories and bodily tension that seemed to gather the minute the environment reminded him of what had happened.

Those same reminders also kept his body and attention in a state of readiness. At work, a loud metallic bang or an unexpected sound in the bay would make him jerk and immediately search the area, and he noticed that once he was keyed up he could not stop scanning for signs of danger. In any building, including restaurants or his church, he was uncomfortable until he had identified the exits and decided how he would get out if something went wrong. The antiseptic smell of clinics was especially potent; even passing a medical office was enough to make him more vigilant, more aware of who was near him, and more likely to react sharply if someone touched him without warning. His wife has learned not to come up behind him because he startles so intensely that he feels embarrassed and angry afterward.

Over time, this constant watchfulness seemed to make the reminders spread. Because Kwame was already scanning his surroundings and mapping escape routes before he felt at ease, ordinary parts of the workplace stood out to him as possible signs of threat. A routine noise he might once have ignored now caught his full attention and felt loaded. When he was tense, even a cleaning product with a sterile scent could register as if it belonged to an emergency room, and he would feel himself transported back into the atmosphere of the exposure. The more alert he stayed, the easier it became for the workplace, loud sounds, and medical smells to set him off again.

His ways of coping have tightened that pattern rather than easing it. By avoiding hospitals and examinations, he gets short-term relief, but he remains convinced those places are unbearable and dangerous to enter. By refusing to be alone, he never has the chance to discover that solitude itself is not the threat he feels it to be; instead he stays on edge whenever separation seems possible. Overworking has narrowed his life further. He takes extra shifts and lingers at work rather than going home early, telling himself it is better to stay occupied than to be left with his thoughts. Yet the fatigue leaves him even more jumpy, more likely to react to a touch on the shoulder, and more dependent on scanning and exit planning to feel barely in control. His wife has begun to complain that even when he is physically home, he is not really with her, just watching the room.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was exhausted by how small and effortful his life had become. He could still function in his highly specialized job, but only by staying in motion and never letting his guard down. What finally brought him in was the recognition that he was organizing every setting around escape, every day around avoiding reminders, and still feeling as if the danger could break through at any moment. He says he wants to stop living "like the leak is still happening." What frightens him most is the possibility that if he stops monitoring and pushing himself, he will be caught off guard again. What he hopes, cautiously, is that he might be able to be in a room by himself, hear an abrupt noise, or walk past a hospital without feeling that his body has already been overtaken.
